questions.title: Walk me through your career so far
questions.body: Common opening question. Expected length: ~2 minutes. Cover arc from start to now and end on why you're moving toward this role.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: 2 minutes max. Arc: TCS (foundations, Verizon kiosk app) → Publicis Sapient Lloyds (digitization, 25 paper forms → digital, +20% revenue, 700ms→150ms perf) → Wowcher (multi-brand architecture for 4 brands, AI-first delivery at Ticketmaster). End on: "And what's pulling me toward AI product engineering is the chance to combine my consumer-scale frontend experience with the AI-first workflow I've already shipped — at a company building the underlying tech."

questions.title: Why are you looking to leave your current company?
questions.body: Asked by every recruiter. Sensitive — frame positively.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Frame around growth, not grievance. "I've delivered the multi-brand migration architecture I was hired to lead — POC live at 50/50 on next.wowcher.ie, June 2026 parity target. The next problems I want to work on are at the intersection of AI and consumer products at scale, which is where companies like [theirs] are operating right now." Never trash the current employer, never mention compensation as the primary reason.

questions.title: Why this company specifically?
questions.body: Asked in every loop. Generic answers ("I love your mission") are graded down. They want specifics tied to your experience.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Three concrete things tied to your experience. Template: "Your [specific product/feature] is solving the exact ergonomic problem I hit on the [your project] — getting [thing] reliable enough for [user type] — and I want to take what I learned there and apply it at your scale." Have a different version of this prepared per target company.

questions.title: Walk me through your most impactful project
questions.body: Standard senior-level prompt. They're listening for: scale, stakes, complexity, your contribution, business outcome.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Use the Wowcher multi-brand migration. Structure: SCALE (1,056 divergent files across 4 brands), STAKES (CEO presentation, 8-phase canary, June 2026 parity target, revenue protection), TECHNICAL DEPTH (Cloudflare Worker for cookie-based canary assignment, blue/green deployment with 2-3 week warm period, normalised revenue ratio for monitoring (MB rev/MB sessions ÷ WUK rev/WUK sessions), brand config folder system replacing env-based resolution), YOUR CONTRIBUTION (architecture design, audit tooling — compare.sh + analyze_diff.py, presented strategy to CEO/CTO), OUTCOME (POC live at 50/50, 50% code duplication cut, new brand launch time 6 months → <1 week).

questions.title: Tell me about a time you used AI to ship something you couldn't have shipped otherwise
questions.body: AI-roles favorite. Probes for production AI experience, judgment, and ownership.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Ticketmaster 3D Map Review. SITUATION: stakeholders needed 3D venue review app, traditional timeline 3+ months. TASK: ship on compressed timeline. ACTION: AI-first workflow, ~90% code AI-generated, my contributions: Three.js + React architecture, prompt iteration, every line code-reviewed, rejected ~20% of AI suggestions, comprehensive test suite, explicit prompt for 'don't invent APIs', verified against docs. RESULT: ~90% faster delivery vs baseline, quality maintained, set template for team. Always emphasize: the AI was a typist, not a thinker. I owned every decision.

questions.title: What's the most senior engineering decision you've made?
questions.body: Probes for Staff-level signal: did you make a call that affected scope, risk, or strategy?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: The blue/green deployment with 2-3 week Wowcher warm period during multi-brand cutover. Hit: ALTERNATIVE (hard cutover, faster, riskier), YOUR RECOMMENDATION (warm period for fast rollback if revenue regresses), TRADE-OFF (infrastructure cost vs revenue protection), HOW YOU CONVINCED (presented to CEO with normalised revenue ratio for monitoring, defined kill criteria), OUTCOME (accepted, set the standard for major rollouts).

questions.title: Describe a time you disagreed with a senior leader
questions.body: Probes for: ability to disagree without being abrasive, courage of conviction, ability to find middle ground.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Real story required. Possibilities: architecture disagreement with Rey, canary threshold conversation with CEO, prioritization debate. Structure: THEIR POSITION, YOUR POSITION, EVIDENCE you brought (data, prior incidents, customer impact), OUTCOME (compromise is fine — "I won" is not required), what you'd DO DIFFERENTLY. Show calibrated disagreement.

questions.title: How do you stay current with frontend in 2026?
questions.body: Probes for genuine curiosity and self-directed learning. "I read Twitter" fails.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Concrete sources, not abstract claims. "I read the Next.js and React core team blogs, follow Anthropic and OpenAI engineering blogs for AI integration patterns, work through Josh Comeau's rendering deep dives, do a question a day from GreatFrontEnd. Most importantly I use new tools in side projects — recently built a CV rewriter with the Claude API and an interview prep PWA. Side projects are where real learning happens."

questions.title: Tell me about a time you mentored someone
questions.body: Probes for leadership and the ability to multiply yourself.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: The offshore team of 15 at Wowcher. Hit: SCOPE (15 devs across multiple workstreams), WHAT YOU DID (coding standards doc, structured review process with checklists, upgrade tasks tracked in SharePoint worklog, enforced PRs-only-after-worklog policy, pairing sessions), OUTCOME (consistent delivery quality, reduced review thrash). If asked to go deeper: pick ONE person and ONE specific moment where you saw them level up.

questions.title: What's a technical opinion you hold strongly but most people disagree with?
questions.body: Probes for first-principles thinking. They want to see how you defend a position.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Have one ready. Examples: "Most teams over-invest in state management libraries — Zustand or useReducer+context wins 80% of the time over Redux." Or: "AI-generated code without an eval suite is a liability, not an asset." Or: "Most React perf problems are state-architecture problems, not memoization problems." Be ready to defend with concrete examples.

questions.title: Where do you see yourself in 3 years?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Show ambition without saying "your job." "Either Staff Engineer leading AI product surface area, or having co-founded something in the AI tooling space. Either way, deep in production AI — not adjacent to it." Tie to their company's progression.

questions.title: What's your salary expectation?
questions.body: Negotiation moment, often happens early. Anchor high, defend with research.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Research first. Senior AI Product Engineer London May 2026: £110-160k base + equity is the band; £140-200k+ at frontier labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind). Anchor at the top of your band: "Based on my research and what I'm seeing for senior frontend engineers with shipped AI experience in London, I'm targeting £150k base. Total comp matters more than base, so I'm flexible on the mix." Don't give a range — give a number. Ranges become floors.

questions.title: Why should we hire you over another senior frontend engineer?
questions.body: Hardest version of "why you." Three differentiators max.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: (1) Shipped AI product end-to-end (Ticketmaster), not just experimented; (2) Led a high-stakes multi-brand migration with CEO visibility; (3) Work across the frontend/infra boundary (canary, Cloudflare Workers, performance, monitoring strategy). End: "You're not just hiring a frontend engineer — you're hiring someone who can own an AI product surface from architecture to deployment."

questions.title: What questions do you have for me?
questions.body: Always asked. Always have 5 ready. Bad questions lose offers; great questions win them.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Strong questions: (1) "What does success look like for someone in this role in their first 90 days?" (2) "What's the biggest technical debt the team is carrying right now?" (3) "How do you decide what to build with AI vs what to keep deterministic?" (4) "What's the team's eval philosophy?" (5) "How does the team work with product / design / research?" (6) "What would make you not extend an offer to a candidate after a strong technical loop?" Bad questions: anything answerable on the website; "how's WLB" (too early); "what tech stack do you use" (too shallow).

questions.title: Tell me about a time you failed
questions.body: Probes for self-awareness. "I work too hard" is a disqualifier.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Real story, real lesson, no humble-brag. Example shape: deployment that broke production, a project that didn't ship, a hire that didn't work out. Structure: WHAT HAPPENED, WHY (root cause analysis, not blame), WHAT YOU LEARNED, HOW YOU CHANGED YOUR PROCESS. The lesson should be transferable, not specific to that one situation.

questions.title: How do you handle ambiguity?
questions.body: Senior+ filter. Junior engineers want clear specs; senior engineers create clarity.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Concrete story. The Wowcher multi-brand audit fits: "When I started on the migration, no one had a clean answer to which files were truly divergent across the 4 brand codebases. So my first move was to build compare.sh and analyze_diff.py — tools to make the ambiguity tractable. Once we could see the 1,056 divergent files categorized by feature-flag vs code-change, the conversation went from speculation to planning." Principle: "When the problem isn't clear, my first move is to build a tool to make it visible."

questions.title: How do you give feedback to a peer whose code you think is weak?
questions.body: Probes for code review style and team health.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Process not personality. "PR comments focused on specific lines with 'here's what I'd consider' framing. If it's a pattern I keep seeing, I'll DM them and offer a quick pairing session — usually framed as 'I want to understand your thinking', not 'let me correct you'. I never make code review personal, and I always praise good code as visibly as I critique weak code."

questions.title: How do you decide what to prioritize when everything is urgent?
questions.body: Probes for executive function and the ability to say no.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Framework. "I separate urgent from important using two axes: blocking revenue, blocking other people, blocking learning. Then I pick the top two and TELL my manager what I'm explicitly deferring — saying no is part of prioritization. If everything is truly urgent, that's a sign of a planning failure earlier in the cycle, and I'll surface that too."

questions.title: What's the difference between a senior and a staff engineer to you?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: "Seniors deliver excellent work on assigned problems. Staff engineers identify which problems are worth solving. Staff multiply other engineers — through architecture decisions that age well, through writing that propagates good thinking, through mentorship that lifts the team's floor. The shift is from execution to leverage."

questions.title: Describe your ideal team culture
questions.body: Probes for fit. Be honest but compatible with their culture.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: "Direct, written-first communication. Low ego in code review. Strong opinions held loosely. Bias toward shipping over polishing. Async-friendly so deep work is possible. Senior engineers who teach, not protect knowledge." Adapt one or two points to the company's published values.

Explain the event loop: macrotasks, microtasks, animation frames
questions.body: Crucial fundamental. Senior interviews go deep.
questions.answer:
ANSWER: Stack runs to empty → drain ALL microtasks (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) → render phase (rAF callbacks, style/layout/paint) → ONE macrotask (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, message events). Then repeat.

Key implications:
- Promise resolves before setTimeout(0) — Promises are microtasks, setTimeout is a macrotask
- A long-running microtask chain can starve rendering (microtask starvation)
- rAF fires before paint, useful for read-then-write DOM patterns
- Event handlers (click, etc.) run their handler, then drain microtasks, THEN the next event
- In React 18+, automatic batching defers state updates until the next microtask

Pitfall: `await` inside a `for` loop with side effects creates a microtask chain that can block rendering.

questions.title: What's the difference between let, const, var? Explain hoisting.
questions.answer: ANSWER: `var` is function-scoped, hoisted with `undefined` initial value. `let` and `const` are block-scoped, hoisted to the top of the block but in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) — accessing them before declaration throws ReferenceError. `const` adds: cannot be reassigned (but the value can still be mutated if it's an object). Function declarations are fully hoisted (name + body); function expressions only the variable.

questions.title: Explain closures with a practical example
questions.answer: ANSWER: A closure is a function that retains access to its lexical scope even when invoked outside that scope. The function 'closes over' the variables it referenced when defined. Example: `debounce` — the `timer` variable lives in the outer function's scope but the inner function continues to access and mutate it across calls. Practical uses: encapsulation (private state via factory functions), memoization, currying, event handlers that need to remember which item they belong to.

questions.title: What happens when you JSON.stringify an object with a circular reference?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Throws `TypeError: Converting circular structure to JSON`. Workaround: pass a replacer function with a WeakSet to track seen objects and emit `[Circular]` placeholders.

questions.title: Explain async/await in terms of Promises
questions.answer: ANSWER: `async` functions always return a Promise. `await expr` pauses the function, schedules the rest as a microtask continuation when `expr` resolves. Mechanically, async/await is sugar over `.then()` chains. Errors in async functions become rejected promises; `try/catch` around `await` catches them.

questions.title: Implement compose(...fns) and pipe(...fns)
questions.body: Functional composition. `compose(f, g, h)(x) === f(g(h(x)))`. `pipe` is left-to-right.

questions.title: What's the difference between Map and Object? When use which?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Map: any key type (object, function), preserves insertion order, has size property, optimized for frequent add/remove, no prototype keys to worry about. Object: string/symbol keys only, JSON-serializable, integrates with prototype chain. Use Map when keys aren't strings, when ordering matters, or when you'll do many add/remove ops. Use Object for static configuration, JSON shapes, and prototypal patterns.

questions.title: Explain microtask starvation with an example
Explain the React rendering pipeline: render phase vs commit phase
questions.answer: ANSWER: Render phase: React calls your function components, builds a new fiber tree by diffing against the current tree. Pure, idempotent, interruptible (Concurrent mode can pause/resume/discard). Commit phase: React applies DOM mutations, runs layout effects (useLayoutEffect), then paint, then passive effects (useEffect). Not interruptible. Strict mode in React 18+ double-invokes the render phase in dev to catch impurity.

questions.title: Difference between useMemo and useCallback. When does each help?
questions.body: Common interview filter — many devs misuse both.
questions.answer: ANSWER: `useMemo` memoizes a value, `useCallback` memoizes a function (sugar over `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`). They help in two cases: (1) the computation is genuinely expensive (rare); (2) the result is a referential dep of `useEffect` or `React.memo` child — if you don't memo, the dep changes every render. Premature use is noise: with shallow comparisons, you pay the cost of memoization on every render whether or not the value changed. The React 19 compiler auto-memoizes — making manual use largely unnecessary in compiler-enabled code.

questions.title: What is useTransition and when do you use it?
questions.answer: ANSWER: `useTransition` marks a state update as non-urgent. The previous UI stays interactive while React works on the new one. Use case: filtering a large list while keeping the input responsive. `const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition(); startTransition(() => setFilter(value));` Compare to `useDeferredValue` which defers a VALUE instead of marking an update.

questions.title: Server Components vs Client Components in Next.js 15. When use which?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Server Components render on the server only, can be async, can directly access data sources, ZERO JS shipped to the client. Client Components hydrate, use hooks, handle events. Use Server by default; opt into Client with `'use client'` only when needed (interactivity, browser APIs, hooks). Server can render Client; Client cannot render Server (only pass as children). Practical: data fetching, layouts, static content → Server. Forms, modals, interactivity → Client.

questions.title: You have a list of 10,000 items and the page is janky. Walk through diagnosis.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: (1) Measure with React DevTools Profiler — identify which component is slow. (2) Decide: is it render count (something causing re-renders) or render cost (each render is expensive)? (3) For render count: investigate referential equality, key stability, parent re-renders. (4) For render cost: virtualization (react-virtuoso, tanstack-virtual). (5) Re-evaluate data: do we need 10k in the DOM at all? Server-side filter? Pagination? (6) If still slow, look at memoization, then offload heavy work to Web Worker.

questions.title: How does React reconciliation handle keys? What goes wrong with index-as-key?
questions.answer: ANSWER: React uses keys to match elements between renders. Same key = same element (preserve state, DOM nodes, refs). Different key = unmount old, mount new. Index-as-key breaks when the list reorders or items are inserted/removed: existing items get reassigned to new positions, their internal state (input values, focus, scroll position) follows the key not the data. Use stable IDs from the data.

questions.title: How do you handle race conditions in useEffect that fires fetches?
What's wrong with this Search component?
questions.answer: ANSWER: (1) No debounce — fires on every keystroke, hammers the API. (2) No abort — out-of-order responses race; user types 'react', responses come back in order 'r', 're', 'react' but in arbitrary order. (3) No loading state. (4) No error handling. (5) No empty-query guard — fetches with `?q=`. (6) Template string URL-encoding issue if query has special chars (use URL/URLSearchParams). (7) Results not rendered — bug or stub?

questions.title: You're upgrading React 17 to React 18. What do you check for breaking changes?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK (YOUR STORY): (1) `ReactDOM.render` → `createRoot` — affects every entry point. (2) Automatic batching now batches updates in promises, setTimeout, native events — tests that asserted on intermediate states may break. (3) StrictMode double-invokes in dev — flushes out effects that mutate during render. (4) Removed `react-dom/test-utils` paths — affects testing setup. (5) Removed string refs. (6) Suspense semantics changed. (7) Concurrent rendering can introduce subtle render order issues. Your real-world story: ESM/CJS conflicts during the move, SSR edge cases, build performance regressions.

questions.title: You're upgrading Next.js 12 to 15. Walk through your strategy.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK (YOUR STORY): (1) Inventory features used — Pages Router vs App Router, middleware, Image, Font, Link API changes. (2) Incremental App Router adoption — page by page, hybrid is supported. (3) ESM/CJS conflicts — major pain point in your real migration. (4) Image component API changes — `layout` prop removed, sizes/srcset model changed. (5) Middleware: Edge runtime, no Node APIs. (6) `next/font` replaces self-hosted fonts. (7) Build perf: turbopack consideration. (8) Test in staging behind a flag before cutover. Mention your normalised revenue ratio monitoring approach.

questions.title: What is Suspense and how does it work with data fetching?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Suspense lets components 'wait' for something before rendering, showing a fallback while waiting. Mechanism: a child component throws a Promise during render; the nearest Suspense boundary catches it and renders the fallback. When the Promise resolves, React retries the render. With Server Components + frameworks like Next.js App Router, async components and `use()` make data fetching declarative. The key shift: data fetching co-located with the component instead of fetching-then-rendering.

questions.title: What's hydration mismatch and how do you debug it?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Server renders one DOM tree, client expects a different one — React errors and falls back to client render. Common causes: rendering `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` (different between server and client), reading localStorage/window (undefined on server), browser-extension DOM injection, locale-dependent formatting, conditional rendering based on `typeof window`. Debug: enable React's hydration error overlay, narrow down by isolating components, use `suppressHydrationWarning` sparingly for known-OK cases.

questions.title: Explain React 19 useOptimistic hook
Build an Autocomplete component
questions.body: Requirements: debounced API calls, keyboard navigation (up/down/enter/escape), ARIA combobox semantics, recent searches, loading state, empty state.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: State: query, results, loading, highlightedIndex, isOpen. Debounce 300ms. AbortController on each fetch. ARIA: role="combobox", aria-expanded, aria-controls, aria-activedescendant. Each option role="option" with id. Keyboard: ArrowUp/Down moves highlight (wrap or clamp — confirm with interviewer), Enter selects highlighted, Escape closes + restores query. On select, blur input or keep open per spec. Persist recent searches in localStorage (last 5). Edge cases: query of just spaces, no results, error from API, slow response after query cleared (abort).

questions.title: Build a Modal with focus trap, ESC to close, click outside, scroll lock, ARIA
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Render in portal (document.body or a designated #modal-root). Trap focus: on open, focus the first focusable inside; on Tab from last → first, Shift+Tab from first → last. Store the trigger element on open, restore focus on close. Scroll lock: `body { overflow: hidden }`, but compensate for scrollbar width to prevent layout shift. ESC: window keydown listener while open. Click outside: backdrop click closes; clicks inside the panel don't bubble. ARIA: role='dialog', aria-modal='true', aria-labelledby pointing to title, aria-describedby pointing to body. Inert the rest of the page (or aria-hidden the siblings).

questions.title: Build a virtualized list of 100,000 rows with real-time filter
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Container with fixed height and overflow:auto. Inner spacer with total height = rowHeight × totalRows. Compute startIndex = floor(scrollTop / rowHeight), endIndex = startIndex + visibleCount + buffer. Render only [start..end] absolutely positioned. Filter: pre-compute filteredItems on each query change. Use `useDeferredValue` on the query so input stays smooth; the heavy filter work runs as low-priority. For variable row heights: position cache with running sum and binary search to find start.

questions.title: Build a streaming chat UI (AI assistant)
questions.body: Highly relevant for AI roles. Often the Anthropic/OpenAI frontend interview.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: State: messages array with role, content, status. Streaming: fetch SSE endpoint, ReadableStream reader, parse `data:` lines, append chunks to the current assistant message's content. UI: virtualized message list (long conversations), autoscroll only when at bottom (sticky behavior), 'New message' chip if user scrolled up. Markdown rendering: re-parse on each chunk (cheap for normal lengths); render code blocks even when ``` is unclosed mid-stream. Stop button: AbortController on the fetch, save partial content to history. Error mid-stream: keep partial, show inline retry. Tool calls: block-based message model — text, tool_use, tool_result are sibling blocks; show tool_use as collapsible cards. Optimistic send: show user message immediately with status='sending'.

questions.title: Build a Kanban board with drag-and-drop, no external libraries
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: State: columns = Map<columnId, Array<cardId>>; cards = Map<cardId, card>. Native HTML5 drag-and-drop: dragstart (set effectAllowed, dataTransfer), dragover (preventDefault to allow drop, compute insertion index by mouse Y vs card centers), dragenter/dragleave (visual feedback), drop (mutate state). Keyboard a11y: each card focusable, space to 'pick up', arrows to move, space again to drop. Edge cases: drop on empty column, drop on self (no-op), dragging while modal open (block). Optimistic UI: mutate immediately, send to server async.

questions.title: Build an infinite-scroll feed
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: IntersectionObserver on a sentinel div at the bottom; when intersecting, fetch next page. State: pages array, hasMore, loading, error. Cursor-based pagination preferred over offset (consistent under inserts). Scroll restoration on back nav: store scroll position + page index in router state. Empty state, loading skeleton (per row), error retry button at the bottom. Don't re-fetch already-loaded pages on mount unless needed. With React Query / TanStack Query: useInfiniteQuery handles this idiomatically.

questions.title: Build a notification toast system
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: API: `toast.success(msg)`, `toast.error(msg)`, `toast.custom(...)`. Implementation: a singleton store (Zustand or context+reducer) with an active toasts array. Top-level `<Toaster />` component subscribes and renders. Each toast has id, message, type, duration, dismissible. Auto-dismiss via setTimeout, cleared on hover (pause on hover). Stack up to N, queue the rest. ARIA: role='status' for info, role='alert' for errors, aria-live='polite'/'assertive'. Animation: framer-motion or CSS transitions on enter/exit.

questions.title: Build a command palette (Cmd+K)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Modal triggered by Cmd+K (Mac) / Ctrl+K (Win). Items: { id, label, action, keywords, group }. Fuzzy search (fuse.js or implement simple fuzzy match). Keyboard nav: arrows move highlight, Enter executes, Tab moves between groups. Recent items pinned at top. Each group has a heading. Sub-commands: selecting an item with subcommands replaces the list with its children, Esc goes back. Performance: virtualize if many commands. ARIA: combobox + listbox pattern.

questions.title: Build an OTP input (6 separate digit boxes)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: 6 input refs in an array. On input: if digit entered, advance focus to next. On backspace in empty box, focus previous and clear. On paste: split clipboard text, fill multiple boxes. Only allow digits (input type='tel' or numeric pattern with key filter). Submit when all filled. ARIA: aria-label per input. autoComplete='one-time-code' for iOS to surface SMS codes.

questions.title: Build a chip / token input (type, Enter, becomes chip)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: State: tokens array. Input: on Enter (and optionally comma, tab), add current text as token. On Backspace in empty input, remove last token. Each token has remove button. Validation per token (email format, etc.). Duplicate handling (reject or merge). Paste handling: split by comma/newline.

questions.title: Build a date range picker
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Two months visible. Drag-select range OR click start, click end. Hover preview between mouseDown and mouseUp. Keyboard nav: arrows move, Enter sets boundary. Disabled dates (configurable). Timezone aware — store as UTC date strings (YYYY-MM-DD), display in user locale. RTL support. ARIA: role='application' for the calendar, aria-selected on day buttons.

questions.title: Build a multi-step form (wizard) with back/next, validation, async submit
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: State: currentStep, form data per step, validation errors. Per-step validation runs on Next. Going back preserves data (don't reset). Step indicator at top. URL sync (?step=2) so refresh keeps state. Async submit with loading state, error display, retry. Confirmation step shows summary. Resume support: localStorage snapshot of current state.

questions.title: Build a comment thread with nested replies
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Recursive component. Data: tree of comments. Collapse/expand per node. Sort by: newest, oldest, top (by score). Reply textarea inline. Edit/delete only for author (check auth). Avatar, timestamp, relative time ('2 hours ago' updates per minute). Deep threads — show 'Continue thread' at depth N to prevent infinite indentation. Markdown rendering with safe HTML.

questions.title: Design an Autocomplete component (system design depth)
questions.body: Discuss architecture, not write code. Apply RADIO framework.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: REQUIREMENTS (local vs remote? max results? recent searches? typo tolerance? mobile?). ARCHITECTURE (input + dropdown + result item; controlled state with optional uncontrolled fallback). DATA FLOW (debounced fetch with AbortController, cache by query, prefetch on focus, optional Trie for local data). INTERFACE (props: source, renderItem, onSelect, minChars, debounceMs, maxResults, value/onChange for controlled). OPTIMIZATION (LRU cache by query, AbortController to cancel in-flight, virtualization if 1000+ results, keyboard navigation, ARIA combobox, no-results state, error state). DISCUSS: typo tolerance — server-side fuzzy (Postgres trgm, ES fuzzy) vs client-side (Levenshtein, BM25). PERFORMANCE: time-to-first-suggestion is the metric; pre-warm with empty-query top picks.

questions.title: Design a Data Table for 100k rows
questions.body: Sticky columns, virtual scroll, sort, multi-filter, column resize/reorder, row selection, export to CSV.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Virtualization (windowed render with overscan). Column resize via drag handle on header (mouseDown → mouseMove computes delta → set column width). Column reorder via HTML5 DnD. Sticky columns: position:sticky on first N columns; complicates virtualization because horizontal scroll. Sort: server-side preferred at 100k; if client-side, sort the indices not the data. Multi-filter: combine into a single predicate; debounced. Selection: track selected IDs in a Set; 'select all' is logical (filter+all) not physical. Export: stream to Blob using a Web Worker for 100k rows. Mobile: collapse to card layout below a breakpoint.

questions.title: Design a Rich Text Editor (block-based, Notion-style)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: DATA MODEL (tree of blocks; each block has type, content, children, attrs). RENDERING (contenteditable per block, NOT the whole doc — gives per-block keyboard and undo handling). SELECTION (custom selection model layered on browser selection; serialize/deserialize to/from DOM Range). UNDO/REDO (operational transform OR immutable snapshots; OT supports collaboration). SLASH COMMANDS (/h1, /code, /image — detect '/' at start of empty block, open menu). KEYBOARD MAP (Enter → new block of same type or paragraph; Backspace at start → merge with previous block; Tab in list → indent). COLLABORATION (CRDT — Yjs — wraps the document state). PERFORMANCE (virtualize long docs, lazy-render images, suspend rendering during typing bursts).

questions.title: Design a Modal component (advanced)
questions.body: Handles nested modals, focus trap, route-based modals, animation lifecycle.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: STACK MODEL — modals tracked in a context-provided stack, only the top one is interactive. ROUTE-BASED — `/photos/123` can either render a modal over the previous page or a dedicated route based on entry (deep link → full page, click → modal). ANIMATION LIFECYCLE — exit animations require keeping the unmounted-tree-but-still-rendered state; framer-motion AnimatePresence pattern. PORTAL — render in a top-level portal; manage z-index globally not per-modal. INERT — set inert on the rest of the page; restore on close. SCROLL LOCK — body overflow:hidden compensating for scrollbar.

questions.title: Design a Toast/Notification system
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: SINGLETON store. QUEUE if stack exceeds max. DEDUP by content+type within a window (don't spam 'Network error'). PRIORITY: errors over info; promote errors above info in the stack. POSITION: configurable per app (top-right, top-center, bottom). HOVER PAUSES auto-dismiss. SWIPE TO DISMISS on mobile. ARIA: role='status' (info), role='alert' (error), aria-live='polite'/'assertive'. PROMISE TOASTS: `toast.promise(p, { loading, success, error })` updates inline. UNDO TOASTS: include action button that calls a provided undo fn.

questions.title: Design a chat application (Slack/Messenger)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: REQUIREMENTS (channels, DMs, threads, presence, typing, files, search, scale to 10k users). ARCHITECTURE (WebSocket for real-time, REST for history, optimistic send + reconciliation, message ordering via server-assigned monotonic timestamp). CLIENT STATE (normalized by channel+message; virtualized message list per channel). SYNC (delta sync on reconnect via last-seen pointer; full-channel resync rare). OFFLINE (queue outgoing in IndexedDB; flush on reconnect). PERFORMANCE (virtualization, message batching for bursts, image lazy load, code-split per channel type). PRESENCE (heartbeat + decay; show 'last seen' fallback). TYPING (throttled event, no persistence). SEARCH (server-side for history; client-side filter for current channel). ACCESSIBILITY (live region for new messages, keyboard nav between channels).

questions.title: Design Google Docs (collaborative editor)
questions.body: Senior+ filter. The real depth is CRDT vs OT.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: REAL-TIME (WebSocket transport, low-latency edits). CONCURRENCY MODEL: choose CRDT (Yjs, Automerge) — peer-to-peer-friendly, no central authority needed, conflict-free by construction; OR OT (Google's choice) — requires server arbitration, slightly more efficient for text. PRESENCE: cursors and selections rendered for each user with name+color, synced via separate ephemeral channel. OFFLINE: edits queue locally, merge on reconnect. PERMISSIONS: ACL on document; read-only mode disables input. COMMENTS: anchored to text ranges; ranges shift as text changes (use markers/anchors that survive edits). VERSION HISTORY: snapshot strategy (periodic + named); rebuild any version by replaying ops. RENDERING: only the viewport's range; image lazy-load.

questions.title: Design a news feed (Twitter/LinkedIn)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: PAGINATION (cursor-based, not offset — handles inserts correctly). RANKING (server-side ML; client receives ranked list with reason chips). INFINITE SCROLL (IntersectionObserver sentinel). PREFETCH (next page when user is N items from end). REAL-TIME (new posts arrive — show 'X new posts' button rather than auto-prepending; prepending breaks reading). VIRTUALIZATION (variable height, position cache). IMAGES (lazy load, blur placeholder, srcset). VIDEO (autoplay on intersection, muted by default, pause when scrolled out, single playing video at a time). COMPOSE (drafts in localStorage). NOTIFICATIONS (Web Push for re-engagement).

questions.title: Design Figma (collaborative design tool)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: MULTIPLAYER (CRDT for the document tree; presence channel for cursors). RENDERING (Canvas/WebGL — DOM can't handle 50k nodes; layer tiling for large canvases). HIT TESTING (spatial index — R-tree or quadtree). UNDO/REDO (per-user history of own operations, not global). NETWORK (binary protocol, delta encoding, compression). LOCAL STATE FIRST then echo to server. PERFORMANCE (offload heavy paths to Web Worker; OffscreenCanvas for rendering). PLUGINS (sandboxed iframe with postMessage API). EXPORT (server-side rasterization for high-res).

questions.title: Design Netflix
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: VIDEO (HLS/DASH for adaptive bitrate; <video> with Media Source Extensions for advanced control). PREFETCH (next-up episode buffered while watching). DATA SAVER mode (lower bitrate on cellular). UI: row-based browse, lazy-load row contents, hero on first row. SEARCH (server-side, autocomplete-style). WATCHLIST (sync across devices). RESUME WATCHING (per-device + cross-device; store last position every N seconds). RECOMMENDATIONS (rows are recommendation 'shelves'; each row fetched independently for cache-friendliness). OFFLINE (downloaded titles, DRM constraints). A11Y (captions, audio description, keyboard nav).

questions.title: Design Amazon (e-commerce PDP + search + cart + checkout)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: PDP (SSG-with-ISR for SEO and speed; price/stock fetched client-side for freshness; image gallery lazy load with priority hint on first image for LCP). SEARCH (server-side; autocomplete via separate fast endpoint; faceted filters preserve URL state). CART (Redux/Zustand normalized; persisted to server for logged-in, localStorage for anon; merge strategy on login). CHECKOUT (multi-step, server-side validated at each step, idempotency keys on payment). PERFORMANCE (Core Web Vitals are revenue-tied; aggressive code-splitting, edge caching, RSC for non-interactive). PERSONALIZATION (recommendations injected via separate endpoint to avoid blocking primary content). A/B TESTING (server-side flag at edge).

questions.title: Design a multi-brand e-commerce platform
questions.body: YOUR STORY. The Wowcher migration in interview form.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK (YOUR STORY): BRAND CONFIG (folder per brand with theme tokens, content, feature toggles, routing rules; replaces env-based brand resolution). FEATURE FLAGS (typed config imported from brands/<brand>/features). EDGE BRAND RESOLUTION (Cloudflare Worker reads cookie/host/path → routes to right backend or sets brand context). SHARED COMPONENT LIBRARY (brand-agnostic primitives styled via CSS vars). BRAND-SPECIFIC OVERRIDES (composition pattern: shared logic + per-brand component for any brand-divergent UI). DEPLOYMENT (canary by brand — Wowcher.com canary at 5%→100% in 8 phases). MONITORING (per-brand: normalised revenue ratio = (MB rev/MB sessions) ÷ (WUK rev/WUK sessions); alerts on regression). BLUE/GREEN (keep old stack warm 2-3 weeks post-cutover for fast rollback). Mention: 1056 divergent files audited via compare.sh and analyze_diff.py, 50% code duplication reduction.

questions.title: Design a real-time collaborative whiteboard (Excalidraw/Miro)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: CANVAS rendering with layer composition. PERSIST shapes as JSON, not pixels. CRDT for shapes (Yjs). PRESENCE for cursors. UNDO/REDO per-user. EXPORT to PNG/SVG. INFINITE CANVAS (pan/zoom; rendering culling outside viewport). PERFORMANCE (debounced re-render, OffscreenCanvas for heavy paths). PLUGINS / EMBEDS (iframe sandbox).

questions.title: Design an AI chat application with multiple models and tools
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: BLOCK MODEL — each assistant turn is array of typed blocks (text, tool_use, tool_result, thinking). STREAMING — SSE or fetch ReadableStream; parse and append per-block. TOOL CALLS — show as collapsible cards; show args, status, result; never partial-render args. MODEL SWITCHER — per-conversation model setting; show capability differences. ATTACHMENTS — upload pipeline with progress; store as base64 or external URL with auth. ARTIFACTS / CODE OUTPUTS — pop-out panel; iframe sandbox if executable. HISTORY — sidebar with conversation list, search, filter, rename, delete, share. SETTINGS PER CONVERSATION — system prompt, model, temperature, tools enabled. COST/TOKEN COUNTER — running tally for transparency. KEYBOARD SHORTCUTS — Cmd+K command palette, Cmd+/ for slash commands, shift+enter for newline. MOBILE — full screen, swipe to see sidebar.

questions.title: Design Notion (block-based docs with databases)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: BLOCK DOCUMENT MODEL (each block has type, props, children). DATABASE VIEWS (table, kanban, gallery, calendar) projected from same underlying data. PERMISSIONS (per-workspace, per-page, inherited from parent). SEARCH (server-side, indexes block contents + properties). OFFLINE (IndexedDB cache of recent pages). SYNC (CRDT or OT; Notion uses operational transforms). PAGE LOAD: progressive — render skeleton, then top blocks, then everything; defer images. EXPORT (markdown, PDF). MOBILE optimizations differ heavily.

questions.title: Universal playbook: how to approach any AI-assisted coding round
questions.body: Reference card. Read this before doing any of the scenario questions.
questions.answer:
METHODOLOGY (the answer):

1. READ FIRST, CODE SECOND. Spend 5-10 mins reading the codebase. List files. Skim each. Understand data flow before touching anything.

2. RUN THE TESTS IMMEDIATELY. See what passes and fails. Failing tests tell you both what's expected and what's broken.

3. STATE YOUR PLAN OUT LOUD before touching the AI. "I'm going to add X to Y, write tests for Z, verify by running A." This gives the interviewer evidence of judgment.

4. USE THE AI AS A TYPIST, NOT A THINKER. "Write me the boilerplate for X" is great. "How should I solve this problem?" is grading-down.

5. VERIFY EVERY AI OUTPUT. Read it. Run it. Check edge cases. Especially watch for HALLUCINATED METHODS in libraries the AI knows less well, INCONSISTENT TYPES, SUBOPTIMAL ALGORITHMS, MISSING EDGE CASES.

6. NARRATE AI INTERACTIONS. "I'm about to ask Claude to scaffold the parser — I expect it to give me a basic regex split, but I'll need to handle quoted strings myself, so I'll review carefully."

7. ITERATE IN SMALL STEPS. Build → test → review → next. Never let the AI generate 200 lines you haven't read.

8. WHEN THE AI IS WRONG, SAY SO OUT LOUD. "The AI suggested Array.prototype.flat but package.json shows Node 14 — I'll do it manually."

WHAT YOU ARE GRADED ON: critical reading of AI output, engineering judgment, narration of reasoning, ownership of every line.

WHAT YOU ARE NOT GRADED ON: how often you use the AI, prompt eloquence, typing speed.

questions.title: Build feature: add 'save for later' to existing e-commerce cart
questions.body: You inherit a Next.js + TypeScript e-commerce app. Files: Cart.tsx, Product.tsx, CartContext.tsx, types.ts. Cart has add/remove/setQty. Implement: move item from cart to saved list and back. UI: 'Save for later' button on cart row; 'Saved for later' section below cart; 'Move to cart' button on saved row.
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. READ. CartContext is a useReducer with actions ADD, REMOVE, SET_QTY. Items keyed by productId. Types.ts has CartItem.
2. PLAN OUT LOUD: "I'll mirror the cart state with a savedItems slice in the same context. Add SAVE_FOR_LATER and MOVE_TO_CART actions. Then UI: button on CartItem row, new SavedItems component below cart."
3. AI PROMPT: "In CartContext.tsx, extend the state shape to include `savedItems: Record<string, CartItem>` alongside `items`. Add reducer cases SAVE_FOR_LATER (move from items to savedItems by productId) and MOVE_TO_CART (reverse). Keep the existing API stable."
4. VERIFY: read output, ensure the existing ADD/REMOVE/SET_QTY still work, add tests.
5. UI: "Now add a 'Save for later' button to the CartItem row that dispatches SAVE_FOR_LATER. Create a SavedItems component that maps over context.savedItems and renders each with a 'Move to cart' button."
6. EDGE CASES: what if user saves the same product twice while it's already in saved? Preserve qty or reset? Confirm with interviewer.
7. PERSIST: extend localStorage serializer to include savedItems.

NARRATE while coding. Don't accept AI's first try blindly — verify the state shape change didn't break the existing types.

questions.title: Build feature: add typing indicators to a chat UI
questions.body: You inherit a chat app with WebSocket already connected. Implement: when other users in the channel are typing, show 'X is typing...' (or 'X, Y are typing...' for multiple).
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. READ. Find the WebSocket message handler. Find the chat component. Identify how messages are added to state.
2. PLAN: "I'll add a 'typing' event type. Client sends it on input change (throttled to once per 3s). Server broadcasts to channel. UI shows recent typers with a 5-second decay."
3. AI PROMPT (CLIENT SEND): "Add a throttled emit of `{ type: 'typing', userId }` on every input change. Use the existing socket instance. Throttle to once every 3 seconds."
4. VERIFY: throttle implementation — does it leading-edge? Decide explicitly.
5. AI PROMPT (CLIENT RECEIVE): "In the WS message handler, add case 'typing': maintain a Map<userId, lastTypingTime>. Add a setInterval that prunes entries older than 5 seconds."
6. UI: render typer list with proper plural ('Alice is typing', 'Alice and Bob are typing', 'Alice, Bob, and 2 others are typing').
7. EDGE: don't show yourself as typing; clear typer when they send a message.

questions.title: Build feature: add auto-complete table of contents to a markdown blog
questions.body: Blog with MarkdownRenderer.tsx that takes markdown string. Implement: TableOfContents component that extracts headings and renders a clickable nav synced with scroll.
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. READ. Renderer uses unified/remark/rehype.
2. PLAN: "I'll add an AST walker that pulls headings with their id. Render as nested list. Use IntersectionObserver to highlight current section."
3. AI PROMPT: "Write a function `extractHeadings(markdown: string): Heading[]` where Heading = { level, text, id }. Use unified+remark-parse, walk the AST for type='heading', generate slug ids using github-slugger."
4. VERIFY: check that the IDs match what the renderer produces — if they don't, nav clicks won't scroll. Look at how the renderer generates IDs and reuse the SAME mechanism.
5. UI: nested list reflecting heading levels. position:sticky in sidebar.
6. SCROLL SYNC: IntersectionObserver on each heading. The 'current' section is the topmost intersecting. Throttle updates.
7. EDGE: duplicate heading text → IDs collide. Slugger handles with -1, -2 suffixes if implemented correctly. Verify.

questions.title: Build feature: add dark mode that respects system preference
questions.body: You inherit a Tailwind app. Implement: toggle in settings, defaults to system, persists across reload.
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. READ. Tailwind config — is `darkMode: 'class'` or `'media'`? If 'media', it auto-follows system. To support user override, change to 'class'.
2. PLAN: "State = 'light' | 'dark' | 'system'. Apply class='dark' on html when computed value is dark. Listen to prefers-color-scheme media query so system mode follows."
3. AI PROMPT: "Write a useDarkMode hook with state 'light' | 'dark' | 'system', defaulting to 'system'. Persist to localStorage. Apply 'dark' class to html element when effective value is dark. Listen to (prefers-color-scheme: dark) changes."
4. VERIFY: SSR safety — useEffect to read localStorage on client. First paint flash: inline a small script in <head> to set the class before React hydrates.
5. EDGE: storage event from another tab → sync across tabs.

questions.title: Build feature: undo toast for destructive actions
questions.body: Existing app with confirm-dialog on delete. Replace with optimistic delete + 5-second undo toast.
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. PLAN: "Optimistic flow: remove from UI immediately, schedule actual API call after 5s. Toast with 'Undo' button. Click undo → cancel pending call, restore. Otherwise → fire delete."
2. AI PROMPT: "Implement an `optimisticDelete(item)` function that: (1) removes from local state immediately, (2) schedules an API call after 5000ms, (3) shows a toast with an Undo button. Undo cancels the scheduled call and restores the item. Returns a promise that resolves when the operation is finalized."
3. VERIFY: race conditions — what if user navigates away while pending? Either commit on unmount or store pending in a context that survives. What about closing tab — fire beacon API or accept loss.
4. EDGE: multiple deletes in quick succession — each has its own 5s timer? Stack them in the toast component? Confirm UX with interviewer.

questions.title: Extend partial: maze solver — BFS exists, add DFS, then Dijkstra, then diagonal movement
questions.body: Codebase has Maze class with grid, start, end, and `bfs()` method that returns shortest path. Extend progressively as interviewer adds constraints.
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
STAGE 1 - DFS:
- Plan: "DFS is a stack instead of queue. Mirror the BFS structure."
- DON'T ask AI for the algorithm. ASK: "Add a method `dfs(start, end)` to Maze with the same signature as bfs but using DFS. Show me the method shape; I'll fill in the algorithm."
- Then implement DFS yourself, narrating. This shows judgment.

STAGE 2 - DIJKSTRA (weighted edges):
- Plan: "Swap queue for priority queue. Track distances. Same structure."
- Check: does Node have a heap? Likely not. AI PROMPT: "Scaffold a min-heap class with push, pop, peek, size. I'll integrate it."
- VERIFY the heap with a quick unit test before using it in Dijkstra.

STAGE 3 - DIAGONAL:
- Just changes the neighbour generation function. AI PROMPT: "Update getNeighbors to include diagonal moves with cost sqrt(2) (or 14 if using integer costs and cardinal=10)."
- VERIFY by running existing tests for cardinal-only; should still pass with diagonal disabled flag.

NARRATE constantly. The interviewer wants to see you doing the algorithmic thinking; the AI does the boilerplate.

questions.title: Extend partial: rate limiter — fixed window exists, add sliding window, then distributed
questions.body: Codebase: RateLimiter class with `allow(userId): boolean`, fixed window of 100 req/min. Extend progressively.
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
STAGE 1 - SLIDING WINDOW (LOG):
- Plan: "Sliding window via log: store timestamps per user, on allow() prune > windowMs old, count, accept if < limit."
- AI PROMPT: "Add `allowSliding(userId): boolean` that uses a sliding window of 60s. Show me the data structure choice; I'll review."
- VERIFY: memory grows with traffic — flag this. Suggest alternative: sliding-window counter (two buckets, weighted).

STAGE 2 - SLIDING WINDOW (COUNTER, memory-efficient):
- Plan: "Two buckets: current minute, previous minute. Weight previous by how far into current we are."
- This is subtle math. Do it yourself. AI can scaffold the structure.

STAGE 3 - DISTRIBUTED (REDIS-BACKED):
- AI PROMPT: "Refactor allowSliding to use Redis for state. Use ZSet of timestamps with ZREMRANGEBYSCORE for pruning and ZCARD for count. Use a pipeline to make it atomic."
- VERIFY: race conditions — multiple instances reading-then-writing creates a TOCTOU bug. Use Lua script or MULTI/EXEC. Discuss this OUT LOUD.
- COST: at high QPS, ZSet operations are expensive. Mention HyperLogLog or token bucket as alternatives.

questions.title: Extend partial: state machine — basic transition exists, add guards and actions
questions.body: Codebase: StateMachine class with states and `transition(event)` method. Extend to support guards (preconditions) and actions (side effects on transition).
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. READ existing API. transition() probably looks up event in current state's transitions and switches.
2. PLAN: "Guards = optional predicate per transition; if returns false, transition rejected. Actions = optional callback fired during transition."
3. AI PROMPT: "Extend the transitions config to optionally include `guard: (context) => boolean` and `action: (context, event) => void`. Update transition() to call guard, skip if false, then fire action before changing state."
4. VERIFY: where does `context` come from? Add context to constructor. What if action throws? Discuss: rollback or commit + log?
5. FOLLOW-UP often asked: hierarchical states (XState-like). Defer unless asked.

questions.title: Extend partial: promise pool — concurrency exists, add priority queue
questions.body: Codebase: PromisePool that runs N tasks at a time. Extend so tasks have priority — high-priority tasks jump the line.
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. READ. Existing uses a FIFO queue (probably just shift() from array).
2. PLAN: "Replace queue with min-heap keyed on priority. When a worker frees, take highest priority pending."
3. AI PROMPT: "Scaffold a min-heap class. I want enqueue(task, priority) and dequeueHighest()."
4. INTEGRATE yourself — that's where judgment shows. AI gives you the heap, you wire it in.
5. EDGE: priorities aren't a global queue between batches — once a task starts, it can't be preempted. Mention this trade-off out loud.

questions.title: Extend partial: event emitter — basic on/off/emit exists, add wildcard listeners
questions.body: EventEmitter has on(event, fn), emit(event, ...args). Add support for `on('*', fn)` (all events) and `on('user.*', fn)` (namespace).
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. READ existing structure: probably Map<event, Set<fn>>.
2. PLAN: "Two extra maps: wildcardListeners (for '*') and patternListeners (for 'a.*' style). On emit, also call all matching."
3. AI PROMPT: "Update emit to also invoke wildcard listeners and any pattern listeners whose pattern matches the event name. Pattern syntax: 'foo.*' matches 'foo.bar' but not 'foo.bar.baz'."
4. VERIFY: pattern semantics — does '*' alone match 'a.b'? Confirm spec. Edge case: same listener registered on both specific and wildcard — should fire twice (or once if dedup is desired).

questions.title: Debug: failing calculator tests
questions.body: Inherited Calculator class. 7 of 12 tests fail. Find and fix.
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. RUN TESTS. Read the failure list. Don't open the code yet — read test names first.
2. Failing test names tell you what's broken: e.g. 'handles parentheses' failing → parentheses not implemented or broken; 'handles negative numbers' failing → sign handling bug.
3. PICK simplest failing test. Read its assertion. Trace through code to find where it diverges.
4. Common bugs: order of operations (multiplication/division before addition), off-by-one (last token skipped), missing edge case (empty input, single operand), floating-point comparison (use Number.EPSILON or toBeCloseTo).
5. DON'T pattern-match a fix from AI — trace first, then fix. Then re-run tests to confirm exactly that test passes without breaking others.
6. NARRATE: "Test 'handles 2+3*4' expects 14. Current returns 20. That tells me operator precedence is missing — let me find where parsing builds the AST."

DO NOT ask AI to "fix all the bugs" — that's the wrong instinct. Use AI to: explain a stack trace, show idiomatic JS for parsing, scaffold a test for an edge case you found.

questions.title: Debug: React app with memory leak — find and fix
questions.body: App grows in memory over time. Profile and fix.
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. REPRO: open Chrome DevTools → Memory → record allocations over time. Click around. See growth.
2. SUSPECT LIST: (a) event listeners not cleaned up in useEffect, (b) intervals/timeouts not cleared, (c) subscriptions to stores not unsubscribed, (d) refs holding stale closures, (e) large objects in state that should be in ref, (f) infinite re-renders causing fiber-tree allocation.
3. AI PROMPT: "Audit this useEffect for cleanup issues" + paste effect — useful for tedious checking.
4. VERIFY each suspect by commenting it out and re-profiling.
5. Most common in 2026: WebSocket onmessage handlers attached but never removed; subscribe to a store in component but no unsubscribe on unmount; setInterval started but not cleared.

DON'T accept AI's first diagnosis without profiling. Memory issues need data, not guessing.

questions.title: Debug: pagination returns duplicate items on rapid page clicks
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. REPRO. Click page 2, immediately click page 3. Observe duplicates from page 2 still rendered.
2. DIAGNOSE: out-of-order fetch responses. Page 2 fetch was slower; page 3 returned first, then page 2 overwrote with page 2 results.
3. FIX OPTIONS:
   - AbortController on each fetch, abort previous on new (preferred)
   - Sequence guard: each request has an ID, only accept response whose ID matches latest
   - React Query / SWR with proper query keys (does the right thing automatically)
4. AI PROMPT: "Add AbortController to this useEffect that fetches page N. Abort on dep change."
5. VERIFY: rapid clicks no longer cause stale renders.

questions.title: Debug: useEffect re-running infinitely
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. Look at the deps array. Most common cause: an object or array dep that's recreated each render.
   ```js
   useEffect(() => {...}, [{foo: 'bar'}])  // new object every render
   useEffect(() => {...}, [items.filter(...)])  // new array every render
   ```
2. Less common: a function recreated each render that's also in deps.
3. FIX: useMemo the object/array, useCallback the function. OR restructure to avoid the dep — e.g., destructure primitive values.
4. AI is useful here: paste the effect, ask "why might this run infinitely?" — AI is usually right because this is a well-known pattern.
5. VERIFY: add a console.log inside the effect, count invocations.

questions.title: Debug: dates display wrong for users outside London
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. Audit: where does the app handle dates? Find every `new Date()`, `getDate()` (LOCAL), `getUTCDate()`, `toLocaleString()`, formatting calls.
2. Common bug: server sends ISO string in UTC; client formats with `toLocaleDateString()` (local timezone) — fine. But somewhere code does `new Date(isoString).getDate()` and stores that as a 'day' — wrong if user is in non-UTC zone.
3. FIX: store UTC everywhere. Format with explicit timezone using Intl.DateTimeFormat or date-fns-tz. Be explicit about which 'day' you mean.
4. AI PROMPT: "Audit this function for timezone bugs" — useful for tedious files.
5. VERIFY: set computer to Tokyo time, reload, see if dates make sense.

questions.title: Debug: tests pass locally, fail in CI
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. Compare environments: Node version, OS, timezone, locale.
2. Common causes:
   - TIMEZONE: tests assume local time. Fix: set `TZ=UTC` in CI; mock Date.
   - RANDOM DATA: tests use Math.random or Date.now. Fix: seed RNG, mock Date.now.
   - PARALLEL POLLUTION: tests share global state (DB, file system, env vars). Fix: isolate per test.
   - TIMING: setTimeout-dependent tests; CI is slower. Fix: use waitFor, avoid fixed timeouts.
   - DEPENDENCY VERSIONS: lockfile vs package.json drift. Fix: `npm ci` not `npm install`.
3. AI PROMPT: "What CI-specific issues could cause this test to fail?" + paste test. Useful for brainstorming.

questions.title: Debug: login redirects in a loop between /login and /dashboard
questions.answer:
PLAYBOOK:
1. Trace: what does each route check? /dashboard checks for token, redirects to /login if missing. /login checks for token, redirects to /dashboard if present. Loop happens when token state is inconsistent between checks.
2. Common causes:
   - Empty string token: one check treats `'' as falsy, another as 'present'.
   - Async state not propagated: token set in localStorage but React state not yet updated when navigation happens.
   - Middleware checks cookie; client checks localStorage. Out of sync.
3. FIX: single source of truth for auth. Loading state during initial auth check — don't redirect until you know.
4. AI is useful to talk through the flow: "explain this auth check" + paste — gets you a checklist of what could go wrong.

questions.title: Meta: 'Why did you choose this AI prompt over another?'
questions.body: Asked during the round when you prompt the AI.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Explain INTENT. Examples: "I gave the exact function signature because I don't want the AI inventing a different API." "I asked it to explain its plan before writing code so I can intervene before it goes off-track." "I scoped the prompt to just the parser logic — I'll handle integration myself because I want to keep that code clean."

questions.title: Meta: 'The AI gave you code that works but doesn't match the codebase style. What do you do?'
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Bring it in line. Mention out loud: "This uses class syntax but the rest of the file uses functions. I'll refactor before submitting. Consistency is part of code quality." Don't just leave it — that signals you don't care about the existing code.

questions.title: Meta: 'The AI confidently claims library X has method Y. You're not sure. How do you check?'
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Don't trust, verify. Options: open the docs in a tab, check node_modules source, write a quick test, or use AI's web-enabled mode for grounding. Out loud: "I'm not familiar with this method — let me check the docs before relying on it." Hallucinated methods are the #1 AI-failure mode in coding rounds.

questions.title: Meta: 'You're stuck. The AI's suggestions aren't helping. What's your move?'
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Stop using the AI for a moment. Restate the problem from scratch — to yourself, then to the interviewer, then maybe to the AI with a fresh prompt. Often the problem is YOUR understanding, not the AI's capability. Better questions yield better answers. If still stuck, ask the interviewer for a hint — that's not a failure, it's a normal interview move.

questions.title: Meta: 'How much should you rely on AI in this interview?'
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: The honest answer interviewers love: "As much as it helps me ship correct code I understand, and no more. I'd write a `for` loop myself; I'd ask AI to scaffold a class hierarchy. The line is: am I learning anything by typing this, or am I just typing?"

questions.title: What is a large language model, in one paragraph?
questions.answer: ANSWER: A transformer-based neural network trained on huge text corpora to predict the next token given a sequence. At inference, it samples tokens one at a time conditioned on the prompt + previously generated tokens. 'Knowledge' is compressed into the weights during training; 'reasoning' is an emergent property of next-token prediction at scale. The model doesn't think, plan, or remember between calls — every API call is stateless except for what you put in the context.

questions.title: What is a token? Why does it matter?
questions.answer: ANSWER: A token is the unit the model operates on — roughly 4 chars or 0.75 words in English. Tokenization uses BPE (byte-pair encoding) or similar. Why it matters: (1) pricing is per-token, (2) context windows are token-bounded (200k Claude, 128k GPT-4), (3) rare words become multiple tokens, hurting both cost and quality, (4) generation latency scales with output tokens.

questions.title: Why do LLMs hallucinate, and what do you do about it?
questions.answer: ANSWER: They hallucinate because they're next-token predictors, not knowledge bases. When asked something they don't have well-grounded weights for, they generate plausible-looking text. Mitigations layered: (1) RAG — give them grounded context from authoritative sources; (2) constrained generation — function calling, JSON schema, structured output; (3) eval-based prompt iteration — measure hallucination rate, iterate; (4) lower temperature for factual tasks; (5) require citations and verify them; (6) for high-stakes domains, route to human in the loop or refuse out-of-scope queries.

questions.title: Explain RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) in one paragraph
questions.answer: ANSWER: Embed user query, retrieve top-k relevant chunks from a vector store, stuff into prompt as context, generate. The model 'knows' facts it wasn't trained on because they're in the prompt. Key benefits: knowledge updates without retraining, citations possible, smaller models can handle complex domains. Key costs: retrieval quality dominates final quality, latency increases with retrieval step, prompt cost increases with context.

questions.title: Walk through a RAG pipeline for customer support over a product manual
questions.answer: ANSWER: INGESTION: parse manual → split into ~500-token overlapping chunks (paragraph-aware) → embed each (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large or open-source like BGE) → store in vector DB (Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector) with metadata (source, section, last_updated). QUERY TIME: embed user query → vector search top-k (10-20) → optionally rerank with cross-encoder (Cohere Rerank or BGE reranker) → format into prompt with citations like '[1] page 23: <chunk>' → LLM generates with instruction to cite → parse citations from output → return answer with linked sources. EVALUATION: golden set of (question, expected sources, expected answer); measure retrieval recall and generation faithfulness.

questions.title: Your RAG system gives wrong answers even when the right chunk is in the vector DB. Diagnose.
questions.answer: ANSWER: Usually retrieval not generation. CHECK FIRST: was the right chunk in top-k? If not: chunking strategy wrong (too big = noisy, too small = no context, no overlap = boundary loss), embedding model wrong domain, query needs rewriting (HyDE: generate hypothetical document for the query then embed THAT). If yes: model in context but ignoring it — try moving to start/end of context (lost-in-the-middle), use stronger instructions ('answer ONLY from the provided context'), require citations to enforce grounding. Always test retrieval and generation INDEPENDENTLY in evals.

questions.title: What's chunking strategy? Trade-offs?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Fixed-size (e.g., 500 tokens): simple, often splits mid-sentence — bad. Recursive (paragraph → sentence fallback): better semantic boundaries — current standard. Semantic (embed sentences, split where similarity drops): best quality, slow. Late-chunking (embed whole doc, chunk after): newest approach, preserves context. Overlap (50-100 tokens between chunks) preserves cross-boundary context at storage cost. Choose based on: doc structure (code? prose? Q&A?), retrieval precision needed, query type (specific vs broad).

questions.title: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
questions.body: Critical question for production AI roles.
questions.answer: ANSWER: Two metric families. RETRIEVAL: recall@k (does the right chunk appear in top-k?), MRR (mean reciprocal rank — how high is it?). Built from a labelled set of (query, correct_chunk_ids). GENERATION: faithfulness (does the answer match the chunk?), answer relevance (does it match the question?), citation accuracy (do citations actually support the claim?). Both can be scored with LLM-as-judge or human review for a sample. Tools: RAGAS, TruLens, Braintrust. Process: 50-200 examples covering the distribution, automate the run, track over time, gate PRs on regression.

questions.title: What's reranking and when do you need it?
questions.answer: ANSWER: A second-stage cross-encoder model that scores query-chunk pairs after initial retrieval. Use when initial top-k retrieval has decent RECALL but the right answer isn't top-1 — reranking surfaces it. Cost: each rerank is one model call per (query, chunk) pair, so it's only practical for small k (10-50). Tools: Cohere Rerank, BGE reranker. Typical pipeline: retrieve top-50 by vector search → rerank to top-5 → send to LLM.

questions.title: Why stream LLM responses to the UI?
questions.answer: ANSWER: PERCEIVED LATENCY. First-token latency might be 500ms; full response 5s. Streaming shows progress immediately, maintaining user trust. UX research shows time-to-first-token matters more than total time. Also: lets the user STOP early if the answer is going wrong, saving cost. And reduces 'is it broken?' anxiety on long generations.

questions.title: Implement streaming in React from an SSE endpoint
The model returns tool calls mid-stream. How do you handle the UI?
questions.answer: ANSWER: BLOCK-BASED MESSAGE MODEL. Each assistant turn is an array of blocks: text, tool_use, tool_result, thinking. Stream into the CURRENT block; when a new block starts, close the old one. Show tool_use blocks as collapsible cards (name + args + status). NEVER show partial tool calls — wait for the block to complete before invoking the tool (partial JSON args are useless). Once tool result comes back, render as a sibling block. UI distinguishes: assistant text (chat bubble), thinking (collapsed by default, optional reveal), tool use (card), tool result (inline data or card).

questions.title: A user wants to stop the stream mid-response. Design the UX and implementation.
questions.answer: ANSWER: UX: 'send' button becomes 'stop' button while streaming. Stop preserves the partial message in history (don't discard). Show partial as complete from the user's perspective but mark internally as 'stopped'. IMPLEMENTATION: AbortController on the fetch — abort cancels the stream. Server-side: if your inference provider supports cancel, propagate it (saves cost). Update the message status from 'streaming' to 'stopped'. Next user message picks up the conversation including the partial.

questions.title: What is function calling? How is it different from giving the LLM access to a tool?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Function calling = the LLM emits a STRUCTURED request to call a function (name + arguments JSON conforming to your schema). Your CODE executes it; you return the result; the LLM continues with the result in context. The LLM does NOT run the function — you do, in a controlled environment. 'Tool' is the broader term that includes function calling, code execution, web search, file ops, MCP servers — any external capability surfaced through the function-calling interface.

questions.title: Design a UI for an agent that calls multiple tools in a loop
questions.answer: ANSWER: TIMELINE VIEW. Each step is a card: tool name, args (collapsed by default), status (running/success/failed), result (truncated with expand). Show progress (step N of estimated M, or just step N). Allow user to: PAUSE the loop, EDIT a step's args and re-run, RETRY a failed step, OVERRIDE a tool result (manually). Streaming: show 'calling X...' then result. Final answer in chat bubble at end. KEY DESIGN: agent transparency builds trust. Hiding tool calls is a red flag for users — they don't trust black boxes.

questions.title: What are the failure modes of agents in production?
questions.answer: ANSWER: LOOPING (calls same tool over and over — token budget exhaustion). DRIFT (forgets goal over long context — periodically re-state in prompt). COST BLOWUP (no budget, no max-iterations). WRONG TOOL SELECTION (calls search when math was needed — better tool descriptions, examples). UNVERIFIABLE CLAIMS (agent did 'something' but you can't tell — require structured output, log everything). HALLUCINATED TOOL OUTPUTS (model invents what the tool returned — strict typing and parsing). CASCADING FAILURE (one bad tool result poisons the rest — validate each step). Mitigations: max iterations, token budgets, eval on tool-selection, traceability via LangSmith/Helicone/Braintrust.

questions.title: How do you debug an agent that gave a wrong answer?
questions.answer: ANSWER: TRACE every step: prompt, tool calls, tool results, model outputs. Use a tracing tool (LangSmith, Helicone, Braintrust, custom). Find the FIRST step where things went wrong — usually a misread tool result or a hallucinated assumption. Then ask: was the prompt clear? Was the tool description sufficient? Was the tool result well-formatted? Did the model have enough context? Fix at the lowest layer (prompt > tool desc > model > guardrail). Add to eval set as a regression test.

questions.title: How do you evaluate an LLM feature you just shipped?
questions.answer: ANSWER: BUILD LABELLED EVAL SET (50-200 examples covering the distribution, edge cases, known failure modes). SCORE OUTPUTS: exact match (for extraction), LLM-as-judge (for open-ended), human review (high-stakes or where automation is unreliable). TRACK METRICS over time. RE-RUN EVALS on every prompt change, model swap, retrieval change. MINIMUM BAR: 30 golden examples scored on every PR. GOAL: regressions caught before production.

questions.title: What's LLM-as-judge and what are its pitfalls?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Use a strong LLM to score outputs of another LLM/system. PITFALLS: position bias (favors first answer in pairwise comparison), verbosity bias (favors longer answers), self-preference (favors its own family — e.g. GPT-4 prefers GPT-4 output), inconsistency (same input → different scores), brittleness (small prompt changes shift scores). MITIGATIONS: randomize position in pairwise, use multiple judges and aggregate, calibrate against human labels periodically, use a stronger judge than the system under test.

questions.title: A chat feature costs £10k/month. Cut it in half without losing quality.
questions.body: Cost optimization question — common at AI scaleups.
questions.answer: ANSWER (in order of impact): (1) SMALLER MODEL for routing or simple turns (Haiku, Gemini Flash, GPT-4o-mini) — often 10x cheaper, fine for classification or simple Q&A. (2) PROMPT CACHING (Anthropic, OpenAI both support) — system prompt is reused, only pay for the dynamic part. (3) CACHE common queries semantically — Redis with embedding-based dedup. (4) CUT PROMPT SIZE — audit system prompt for fluff, tighten RAG context budget. (5) BATCH where latency allows (Anthropic Batch API: 50% off). (6) SWITCH PROVIDERS — Gemini often cheapest for parity quality; open-source via Together/Anyscale for scale. (7) STREAMING reduces wasted tokens (user stops early).

questions.title: First-token latency is 2 seconds. Users complain. What do you do?
questions.answer: ANSWER: DIAGNOSE LAYERS: network (CDN, edge?), API queue (provider-side), model TTFT itself. MITIGATIONS: (1) EDGE DEPLOY — Cloudflare AI, Vercel AI SDK, Modal for proximity to user. (2) PROMPT CACHING — system prompt cached at provider cuts TTFT significantly. (3) SMALLER MODEL for first response, optionally hand-off — 'Let me think about that' from fast model while slow model works. (4) STREAMING — perceived latency = TTFT, not total time. (5) SPECULATIVE EXECUTION — fire requests early on partial user intent. (6) Check for token-per-input scaling — long prompts have longer TTFT.

questions.title: A medical app uses an LLM. How do you reduce harm?
questions.body: Safety question — Anthropic specifically loves this.
questions.answer: ANSWER: LAYERED DEFENSE. (1) RAG over verified medical sources, NEVER the model's parametric memory for facts. (2) Citation requirement — every claim links to a source. (3) Refuse out-of-scope queries via input classifier. (4) Refuse to give medical advice — route to disclaimer + 'consult a doctor' + emergency phone numbers where appropriate. (5) Output classifier for confidently-wrong patterns (low-confidence hedging, dangerous instructions). (6) Aggressive eval set including red team prompts and known dangerous patterns. (7) Human-in-the-loop for any output that will be acted upon. (8) Legal review of system prompt. (9) Log everything (with privacy in mind) for postmortems.

questions.title: A user is jailbreaking your assistant to write malware. How do you respond at the system level?
questions.answer: ANSWER: LAYERED. (1) INPUT CLASSIFIER refuses before generation — fast and cheap. (2) SYSTEM PROMPT with explicit refusals for malware, weapons, etc. — but don't rely solely on this, it can be bypassed. (3) OUTPUT CLASSIFIER refuses after generation if something slipped through. (4) RATE LIMIT suspicious accounts (many refusals = suspicious). (5) LOG and review patterns for new attacks. (6) Don't rely on one layer — defense in depth. (7) Trust the model's training (Anthropic, OpenAI invest heavily in refusal training) but verify with red team. (8) Customer notification if patterns suggest compromise.

questions.title: What's chain-of-thought prompting? When does it help?
questions.answer: ANSWER: 'Think step by step' — model writes its reasoning before the final answer. Helps on math, multi-step logic, and tasks where the answer benefits from intermediate work. With REASONING MODELS (o1, Claude thinking variants, DeepSeek R1), CoT is built into the model — happens in 'thinking tokens' before the response. With base models, EXPLICIT CoT (asking for steps in the prompt) is still useful and improves accuracy substantially on reasoning benchmarks. Caveat: increases token cost; for simple tasks, no benefit.

questions.title: You change a prompt and accuracy drops. How do you debug?
questions.answer: ANSWER: RUN EVAL SET before and after — you can't manage what you can't measure. Look at WHICH EXAMPLES REGRESSED (vs which improved). Compare DIFFS between old and new prompts. Common causes: removed an anchoring example (few-shot regression), introduced a constraint that confuses the model, reordered instructions and model now follows different ones, added jargon the model interprets differently. Fix: revert and add one change at a time, re-eval each. This is why a 30-example minimum eval set is non-negotiable.

questions.title: How would you A/B test two prompts in production?
questions.answer: ANSWER: FEATURE FLAG per user — stable assignment so a user doesn't bounce between prompts. LOG inputs, both outputs (compute both for fair comparison or accept asymmetric data), USER-VISIBLE METRIC (clicked, copied, regenerated, downvoted), INVISIBLE METRIC (cost, latency, refusal rate). Run for STATISTICAL POWER — calculate sample size in advance based on expected effect. Use chi-square or sequential test (avoid peeking). Watch for NOVELTY EFFECT — early users behave differently, run for a week minimum.

questions.title: What's the difference between an 'AI engineer' and a 'frontend engineer who uses AI'?
questions.answer: ANSWER: AI engineer OWNS the LLM-facing layers: prompt design, retrieval architecture, tool definitions, evaluation framework, cost/latency optimization, agent design. Frontend engineer who uses AI BUILDS product surfaces on top of those layers — streaming UI, tool-call UX, mobile chat, error states. The best teams have BOTH, or one person who can do both — which is what I'm positioning as. My Ticketmaster project required both: I designed the prompts and the UI; I evaluated outputs and shipped the React.

questions.title: Explain prompt caching and when it helps
questions.answer: ANSWER: Provider feature (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini all support variants) that caches the static prefix of the prompt (system prompt, RAG context, etc.) so subsequent calls skip re-processing. Cuts cost by 50-90% on cache hits and improves TTFT significantly. Use when: system prompt is large and reused, RAG context is reused across turns, agent has a long history. Cache TTL is short (5 min Anthropic; cached at server until eviction). Doesn't help if every call is unique.

questions.title: What's MCP (Model Context Protocol) and why does it matter?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Open protocol from Anthropic for connecting AI assistants to external systems (data sources, tools, APIs). Standardizes how an LLM-powered app discovers and calls external capabilities.
