Why it matters: instead of every AI app reimplementing connectors to Google Drive, Slack, GitHub, etc., they speak MCP and connect to any MCP server. For frontend: lets you build an assistant once that adapts to whatever the user has connected. Increasingly being adopted across the industry — supported in Claude, increasingly in Anthropic's competitors.

questions.title: What is a hybrid search and why use it?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Combines vector (semantic) search with keyword (lexical, BM25) search. Catches cases where keywords matter (product names, error codes, dates, code identifiers) that pure embeddings miss. Vector search alone misses 'XF7-2024' if no XF7 in training. Keyword search alone misses 'how do I' phrasings. Combine: run both, fuse scores via reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) or a learned reranker. Modern vector DBs (Weaviate, Vespa, Elasticsearch) support hybrid out-of-the-box.

questions.title: Should you ship without evals?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Almost never for AI features. Without evals: regressions go undetected, prompt changes are vibes-based, you can't make data-driven model swaps, you can't measure improvement, debugging is anecdotal. MINIMUM BAR: 30 golden examples scored on every PR. Better: 200+ examples, automated, gating CI. Counter-argument: very early prototypes where the goal is direction-finding — fine to skip until you know what you're building. But ship to production without evals = ship a feature you can't maintain.

questions.title: Walk through optimizing a slow React page. What do you check first?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: MEASURE, DON'T GUESS. (1) Lighthouse → which Core Web Vital is bad (LCP, INP, CLS)? (2) React DevTools Profiler → which components are slow or re-rendering too often? (3) Network tab → blocking requests, large bundles, slow API. (4) Performance tab → long tasks, layout shifts, main-thread blocking. Then optimize the biggest offender. Don't pre-optimize. Always re-measure after each change.

questions.title: What is INP and how is it different from FID?
questions.answer: ANSWER: INP (Interaction to Next Paint) measures the SLOWEST interaction across the entire page lifetime — typing, clicks, taps. FID measured FIRST interaction only. INP reflects real user pain better. Improve INP by: breaking up long tasks (scheduler.yield, setTimeout chunks), isolating heavy work in Web Workers, using useTransition for non-urgent updates, avoiding synchronous layout reads after writes.

questions.title: LCP is 4 seconds. Walk through diagnostics.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: IDENTIFY THE LCP ELEMENT (Lighthouse shows it). Most common: large hero image. FIX: <Image priority /> hint, preload link in head, srcset for responsive, modern format (AVIF/WebP), CDN. Other causes: render-blocking CSS/JS (defer/async), slow server response (TTFB > 1s — server-side issue or no CDN), late-loaded fonts (font-display:swap), client-side rendering of LCP (move to SSR).

questions.title: You're using Next.js. The build size is 5MB. How do you cut it?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: `next build` shows per-route bundle size. (1) Identify heaviest bundles. (2) Dynamic import non-critical components (modals, charts, editors). (3) Replace heavy libs: moment → date-fns; lodash → modular imports or native. (4) Audit dependencies with `npm ls` or depcheck — find unused. (5) Tree-shaking: ensure libs are ESM and side-effect-free. (6) Remove polyfills if browser target excludes old browsers. (7) RSC for non-interactive — zero JS shipped. (8) Code-split per route via App Router.

questions.title: Multi-brand site: how do you avoid shipping all 4 brand bundles to every user?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK (YOUR STORY): PER-BRAND BUILD via Vercel/CloudFront brand-specific deployments. EDGE BRAND RESOLUTION: Cloudflare Worker resolves brand from cookie/host/path, sets a header. Subdomain or path-based per brand. Conditional dynamic imports keyed on brand — `if (brand === 'superbreak') import('./Superbreak')`. Build-time DEAD CODE ELIMINATION via process.env.BRAND. Separate CDN paths so caching is brand-isolated. Net effect: a Wowcher user never downloads Superbreak JS.

questions.title: Scroll-heavy page drops frames. Diagnose.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: LONG TASKS during scroll. Common causes: (1) onScroll handler doing layout reads (offsetTop, getBoundingClientRect) — these force synchronous layout. Fix: throttle to rAF, or use IntersectionObserver/ResizeObserver instead. (2) React state updates on every scroll → big re-renders. Fix: useDeferredValue on scroll-derived state, or move the state out of React (ref + manual DOM). (3) Non-composited animations (top/left transitions). Fix: use transform/opacity, will-change. (4) Passive listener missing — Chrome warns. Fix: { passive: true } on the listener.

questions.title: A page has high CLS. Most common cause?
questions.answer: ANSWER: Images without width/height attributes (or aspect-ratio CSS). Browser can't reserve space, content shifts when image loads. Other causes: fonts swapping (FOIT/FOUT) — set font-display:optional or preload critical fonts; late-injected banners/ads/cookie notices — reserve space or use position:fixed; dynamically-loaded above-the-fold content — use skeleton placeholders with same dimensions.

questions.title: Review this PR (interviewer shows a diff)
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK CHECKLIST: (1) CORRECTNESS — does it do what the PR claims? Edge cases handled? (2) TESTS — covered? Edge cases tested? Snapshot vs behavior tests? (3) SECURITY — XSS in any HTML rendering? Injection in queries? Auth checks present? Secrets not committed? (4) PERFORMANCE — regressions? N+1 queries? Unnecessary re-renders? (5) ACCESSIBILITY — keyboard nav? ARIA? contrast? focus management? (6) READABILITY — naming, complexity, dead code, consistency with codebase. (7) ERROR HANDLING — async errors caught? user-facing errors clear? (8) OBSERVABILITY — logs/metrics added for new flow? Lead with the big things; nits at the end.

questions.title: What's wrong with this component?
questions.answer: ANSWER: (1) Missing `key` — React warning, breaks reconciliation. Fix: `<User key={u.id} ... />`. (2) Inline function on each render — recreated each time; if User is React.memo'd, breaks memo. Fix: useCallback or move handler up. (3) No fragment wrapper — `.map` returns array, fine in JSX but unusual without wrapper. (4) No empty state — `[]` renders nothing. (5) `users` not defaulted — crashes if undefined. Fix: `users = []` in destructure. (6) No error boundary suggestion. The interviewer wants to see you spot multiple issues and prioritize.

questions.title: A test is flaky. How do you fix?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: REPRODUCE first — run it 100 times to find the failing case (Jest --runInBand --runs=100, Vitest similar). Don't retry your way out — fix the cause. Common causes: TIMING (real timers when fake should be used; missing await; fixed sleeps instead of waitFor). NETWORK (real requests; mock them). RANDOM (seed the RNG). TEST POLLUTION (shared mutable state — DB, modules, window). DOM CLEANUP (afterEach unmount). Add the fix as a regression test that fails before, passes after.

questions.title: Walk through a security review of an LLM chat UI
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: (1) XSS — markdown rendering must allow-list HTML tags (no <script>, no event handlers); render code as text only. (2) PROMPT INJECTION — treat user input as content not instructions; system prompt isolated from user input; instructions for the model in clear hierarchy. (3) DATA LEAKAGE — don't echo PII into logs; rate-limit per-user prompts; ensure RAG retrieval respects ACLs (user can only retrieve their docs). (4) CSRF on history endpoints (mutation-style). (5) RATE LIMITING — cost protection (block runaway loops). (6) AUTH — tokens scoped, refresh handled, no JWT in URL. (7) DRM/CONTENT — don't echo back system prompts (some apps hide them as 'secret'). (8) AUDIT LOGGING — who did what when.

questions.title: Bug hunt: navigate this codebase, find the bug
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: This is Apple's signature format. (1) Read the README/spec to understand intended behavior. (2) Run the app, observe the bug. (3) Form a hypothesis BEFORE diving into code — narrows search. (4) Use the debugger or strategic console.logs to confirm/refute. (5) Read the suspect code carefully — the bug is usually subtle (off-by-one, missing await, wrong dep, race condition). (6) Fix, verify all manual cases, then write a test that would have caught it. (7) Look for SIMILAR bugs elsewhere — Apple loves candidates who find adjacent issues.

questions.title: REST vs GraphQL vs tRPC. When use which?
questions.answer: ANSWER: REST: simple, cacheable, language-agnostic, ubiquitous. Best for public APIs, simple CRUD, when client needs vary independently of server. GRAPHQL: flexible queries, no over/under-fetching, strong typing, single endpoint. Best for complex client-driven views (mobile + web with different needs), federated data, big teams. tRPC: typesafe RPC between TypeScript client and server, no schema layer. Best for full-stack TS apps, internal APIs, fast iteration. Decision: if BOTH ends are your TS code → tRPC. If many clients or external consumers → REST or GraphQL.

questions.title: WebSocket vs SSE vs polling. Trade-offs?
questions.answer: ANSWER: WEBSOCKET — full-duplex, persistent, both sides push. Best for chat, collaboration. Cost: stateful connection, harder to scale, requires sticky sessions. SSE — server → client only, over HTTP, simple. Best for streaming text (LLM responses!), notifications. Reconnects automatically, works through proxies, no special server. POLLING — client requests periodically. Simple but wasteful. LONG POLLING — request held open until update. Fallback when WS not available. For LLM streaming, SSE is the standard.

questions.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic updates. Failure modes?
questions.answer: ANSWER: OPTIMISTIC — assume server will accept, update UI immediately, reconcile on response. Pros: snappy UX. Cons: when server rejects, must revert with explanation; complex state if many ops in flight; harder to keep cache consistent. PESSIMISTIC — wait for server, then update. Pros: simple, consistent. Cons: feels slow. Hybrid: optimistic for low-risk ops (like, comment), pessimistic for high-stakes (payment, delete). Failure modes for optimistic: (1) rollback UX is jarring; (2) cascading state if other UI depends on the optimistic value; (3) reconciliation conflicts if server modifies the entity differently.

questions.title: Explain CORS and the most common gotchas
questions.answer: ANSWER: Browser security: scripts can't read responses from different origins (scheme+host+port) unless the server explicitly opts in via Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. Preflight: complex requests (non-simple methods, custom headers) trigger an OPTIONS preflight; server must allow the method/headers. GOTCHAS: (1) credentials require explicit ACAO+credentials:true AND specific origin (not *). (2) Wildcard ACAO doesn't apply to non-GET non-POST. (3) S3 buckets often forget CORS for SPAs. (4) Cookie SameSite=Strict blocks cross-site even with CORS. (5) Subdomains are cross-origin unless you set document.domain (deprecated).

questions.title: What's a JWT and what are its drawbacks?
questions.answer: ANSWER: JSON Web Token — signed (or encrypted) JSON containing claims. Used as a stateless auth token. PROS: stateless verification (no DB lookup), easy to share between services. DRAWBACKS: (1) Can't revoke without a blocklist (defeating stateless benefit). (2) Tokens grow with claims; cookies have size limits. (3) Algorithm confusion attacks if library accepts 'none' or HS256 instead of RS256. (4) Storage problems: localStorage is XSS-vulnerable; cookies need CSRF protection. (5) Refresh-token rotation complexity. Modern preference: short-lived JWT + httpOnly refresh cookie, or just session cookies.

questions.title: You're brought into a team where the codebase is a mess. 30+ engineers, no tests, mixed React versions, three state libraries. What's your 90-day plan?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: WEEK 1-2: LISTEN. Pair with engineers, read PRs, understand which messes hurt vs which are tolerable. Write down everything but DON'T propose changes yet. WEEK 3-4: MEASURE. Set up baseline metrics (build time, bundle size, test coverage, time-to-deploy, MTTR). WEEK 5-8: PICK ONE THING. The painful-est blocker. Make a small, visible, defensible improvement. Get a win. WEEK 9-12: STAGE THE REST. Propose a 6-month plan with phases, ordered by ROI/risk. Build coalition with seniors before announcing. PRINCIPLES throughout: never trash the existing code in front of the team; credit the engineers who came before; small wins build trust for bigger changes.

questions.title: How do you decide build vs buy?
questions.answer: ANSWER FRAMEWORK: (1) IS IT CORE TO YOUR PRODUCT? If yes, build. If no, buy. (2) WHAT'S THE TCO? Build = engineering time + maintenance + opportunity cost. Buy = license + integration + lock-in risk. (3) WHAT'S THE QUALITY GAP? Mature vendors often outperform internal v1. (4) HOW FAST DO YOU NEED IT? Buy = weeks; build = months. (5) WHAT'S THE STRATEGIC POSITION? Buy where the market is commoditized; build where you have an advantage. (6) WHAT'S THE EXIT PATH if you change your mind?

questions.title: Walk me through the riskiest engineering decision you've made.
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK (YOUR STORY): Wowcher canary rollout strategy. Hit: RISK (revenue regression during cutover for £M revenue/day brand), DECISION (5%→100% canary in 8 phases, normalised revenue ratio for monitoring, blue/green with 2-3 week warm period for rollback), TRADE-OFFS (infrastructure cost vs revenue protection; speed vs safety), HOW YOU CONVINCED CEO (data on similar industry cutovers, defined kill criteria, rollback plan rehearsed), OUTCOME (POC live at 50/50; canary phases meeting thresholds).

questions.title: A senior engineer on your team is hostile to AI tooling. Blocks PRs with AI-generated code. What do you do?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Don't escalate or shame. (1) UNDERSTAND THEIR POSITION — 1:1, ask why. Possible reasons: security concerns, quality concerns, philosophical, fear of obsolescence. All legitimate. (2) NEGOTIATE GUARDRAILS not BANS. Maybe: AI-generated code must be marked, must have human-written tests, must pass extra review. (3) MEASURE — track defect rate of AI-assisted vs human PRs. Bring data to the next conversation. (4) BUILD COMMON GROUND — agree the goal is good code, not pro-AI or anti-AI. (5) ESCALATE only if blocking the team after good-faith effort.

questions.title: Your team is split on Tanstack Query vs SWR. As tech lead, how do you decide?
questions.answer: PLAYBOOK: Frame as PROCESS not OPINION. (1) Criteria: maintainership/funding, ecosystem fit, ergonomics for our use case, team familiarity, migration cost. (2) Score both on each criterion. (3) Build a small spike (1-2 days) if undecided — try a real feature in each. (4) Document the decision (Architecture Decision Record / ADR) with the alternatives considered and why this one. (5) Commit and move on. Bike-shedding kills momentum.

stories.title: Wowcher Multi-Brand Migration (HEADLINE STORY)
stories.situation: Wowcher's e-commerce platform served the Wowcher UK brand on a monolithic Next.js codebase. The business wanted to launch new brands (Metro Deals, Things To Do, 5PM, continue Superbreak as a travel brand) but each spin-up took ~6 months due to tight coupling to Wowcher-specific assumptions in env vars and content.
stories.task: Re-architect into a multi-brand shared codebase. Reconcile ~1,056 divergent files across parallel codebases. Hit feature parity by June 2026 with zero revenue regression.
stories.action: Built compare.sh and analyze_diff.py to categorize the 1,056 divergent files into flag-only, flag+code, and code-only differences. Designed brand config folder system (brands/<brand>/features) replacing env-based brand resolution. Presented 15-slide migration strategy to the CEO: 8-phase canary rollout (5%-100%) with normalised revenue ratio for monitoring — (MB rev / MB sessions) divided by (WUK rev / WUK sessions). Designed blue/green deployment with Wowcher kept warm 2-3 weeks for fast rollback. Built Cloudflare Worker for cookie-based canary assignment. Processed PR audit spreadsheet (469 rows) categorizing 411 PRs into 37 functional areas. Led offshore team of 15 with structured review process and SharePoint worklog enforcement.
stories.result: POC live at 50/50 on next.wowcher.ie. New brand launch time reduced from 6 months to under 1 week. ~50% code duplication cut. CEO-level visibility. June 2026 parity target on track.
stories.metrics: 1,056 files audited; 50% code duplication reduction; 6 months to under 1 week new brand launch; 8-phase canary rollout; 15-developer offshore team led; 411 PRs categorized.

stories.title: Ticketmaster AI-First Delivery
stories.situation: Stakeholders needed a 3D Map Review Application for venue review. Traditional delivery timeline 3+ months. Team had no prior 3D-in-React experience.
stories.task: Ship on compressed timeline while maintaining code quality and shipping a maintainable tool.
stories.action: Designed AI-first workflow with Claude as primary code-gen tool. Architecture decisions (Three.js + React + state model) made by me, not the AI. AI used for: scaffolding, generating test fixtures, writing tests, exploring Three.js APIs. Every line code-reviewed; ~20% of AI suggestions rejected. Explicit prompts for 'don't invent APIs'; verified references against docs. Comprehensive test suite. Pair-prompted with another engineer on hardest sections.
stories.result: ~90% faster delivery vs traditional baseline. Quality maintained, no production incidents. Set template for AI-first workflows at the team.
stories.metrics: ~90% AI-generated code; ~90% faster delivery; ~20% rejection rate.

stories.title: Lloyds Digitization of Banking Forms
stories.situation: Lloyds Bank had 25 paper-based processes for high-value customer requests. Each took days; error-prone; required physical handling.
stories.task: Digitize the journeys end-to-end, reduce turnaround from days to hours, maintain regulatory compliance.
stories.action: Led end-to-end web development for digital banking journeys. Implemented role-based access control. Designed self-service flows. Performance optimization (code-splitting, lazy loading, caching) reduced key web service request from 700ms to 150ms. Raised testing coverage from 15% to 90% on main project; up to 99% on others. Collaborated on 20+ wireframes with UX/UI.
stories.result: +20% revenue from faster turnaround. Days to hours. +15% user engagement. 700ms to 150ms on critical request path.
stories.metrics: 25 forms digitized; +20% revenue; 700ms to 150ms; 15% to 90% test coverage; +15% engagement.

stories.title: Mentoring the Offshore Team of 15
stories.situation: 15-developer offshore team at Wowcher. Code quality varied; reviews dragged; merging felt risky.
stories.task: Raise quality bar across the team and reduce review thrash without micromanaging.
stories.action: Wrote coding standards doc. Set up structured review process with checklists. Tracked upgrade tasks in SharePoint worklog. Enforced 'no PR approved until logged' policy. Ran pairing sessions framed as 'I want to understand your thinking' not 'let me correct you'. Praised good code as visibly as critique weak code.
stories.result: Consistent quality across team. Reduced review cycles. Engineers leveled up.

stories.title: Performance Optimization: 700ms to 150ms
stories.situation: Lloyds web service taking 700ms per request. Multiple teams had touched it; no one owned the perf problem end-to-end.
stories.task: Cut latency materially and prevent regression.
stories.action: Profiled end-to-end with DevTools + backend tracing. Identified bottlenecks: oversized payloads, sync DB calls in middleware, missing CDN cache. Implemented HTTP caching, code-splitting, lazy loading. Renegotiated payload size with backend. Added monitoring for regression prevention.
stories.result: 700ms to 150ms (78% reduction). +15% user engagement. Created team perf playbook.

stories.title: Production Incident: Token / Basket Mismatch
stories.situation: Live production incident at Wowcher: items disappearing from baskets after login; session tokens occasionally not matching basket service. Revenue at risk; support tickets spiking.
stories.task: Diagnose root cause, ship fix, post-mortem.
stories.action: Reproduced across browsers, narrowed to specific flow combinations. Traced request chain — identified race condition between session refresh and basket sync (~50ms stale token window). Designed fix: token version in headers, basket service rejects stale-version requests, client retries with fresh token. Deployed behind flag at 10%, verified, promoted to 100%. Blameless post-mortem; added contract tests for token rotation.
stories.result: Resolved within SLA. Post-mortem informed cross-service contract tests. No recurrence.

companies.name: Anthropic
companies.loopStructure:
Total: 7-9 rounds across 1-4 months. Two onsite loops on separate days; second loop cancelled if you don't pass the first.

1. Recruiter screens (30 min, sometimes split into 2): background, motivation, AI safety alignment.
2. Online Assessment (90 min CodeSignal, or 60 min live): typically 2 multi-part problems building a small system from scratch (e.g., in-memory database with SET/GET/DELETE then filtered scans then TTL then file compression).
3. Hiring Manager Screen (45-60 min): engineering judgment, codebase analysis, scale discussion — NOT live coding.
4. Virtual Onsite Loop 1 (2-3 rounds): coding (build-from-scratch, in-memory db style), system design (LLM infra, GPU scheduling, distributed scale).
5. Virtual Onsite Loop 2 (3-4 rounds): more coding, frontend round (streaming chat, MCP tool-call UI), behavioral, values/culture round (the most common failure point).
companies.notes:
Watch out for:
- Culture/values round is the #1 failure mode. Read Anthropic's published views on AI safety before the onsite. Recruiters share materials; engage with them and form opinions. Expect 3-4 levels of follow-up.
- Concurrency comes up across multiple rounds.
- Coding is first-principles. They may ask you to defend complexity choices and reimplement data structures from scratch after solving cleanly.
- Frontend rounds test streaming UX, MCP tool-call UIs, latency awareness.
- Python is the default language; TypeScript for frontend rounds.

Your edge: Ticketmaster AI-first story is exactly what they hire for. Multi-brand migration shows senior architectural maturity. Prepare to discuss safety trade-offs in your own work.

Failure question to prep: 'Tell me about a time you raised an ethical concern at work or pushed back on a decision.'

companies.name: OpenAI
companies.loopStructure:
Total: 4-6 weeks; sometimes 8-12 for staff+.

1. Recruiter Screen (30-45 min): mission alignment with AGI safety.
2. Technical Screen (60 min): progressive 'gate' format — one problem gets harder over 4 stages. Pass at least 2 to advance. Reported examples: Snapshot Array, Time-Based KV Store, efficient Tokenizer, sliding-window Rate Limiter.
3. Work Trial / Take-Home (48 hours): real engineering project (e.g., webhook delivery system). Evaluated on reliability, code quality, testing.
4. Technical Deep Dive (60-90 min): walk through take-home OR past project.
5. Final Onsite (4-6 hours, 4-6 rounds): coding, system design, project presentation, behavioral. Senior loops add code refactoring round and cross-functional communication round.

Frontend roles specifically: streaming chat UI, browser performance profiler, OpenAI Playground design. Tests practical browser engineering, not React syntax.
companies.notes:
Watch out for:
- Progressive gates: clean working code at each stage beats rushing all 4.
- State management, versioning, memory-efficient data handling are recurring themes.
- Constraints added mid-solve ('now make it thread-safe').
- Mission alignment matters. Read OpenAI's Charter and recent safety blog posts.
- Frontend tests streaming, real-time state, network fundamentals. Be ready on SSE, fetch streams, abort patterns.
- Compensation is exceptional (£140-200k+ base for senior + equity).

Your edge: AI-first delivery + perf stories (700ms to 150ms) align with their practical engineering bar.

Prep specifically: practice the progressive-gate format. Build Time-Based KV store, LRU cache, sliding-window rate limiter. Walk through each level out loud before moving on.

companies.name: Apple
companies.loopStructure:
Total: 4-8 weeks. 5-8 round onsite. Team-based hiring — each team has its own bar.

1. Recruiter Screen.
2. Coding Assessment (sometimes): 20 multiple-choice + small coding tasks under tight time limit.
3. Technical Phone Screen (60 min): React output-based questions, small component builds, vanilla JS depth.
4. Onsite Loop (5-8 rounds, marathon day):
   - JavaScript / Coding: vanilla JS heavy, DOM-related, polyfills (debounce, throttle, deepClone, EventEmitter).
   - Bug Hunt: working on an existing codebase, find and fix bugs. Apple's signature round.
   - Web Performance: LCP, INP, CLS, rendering pipeline, when to use which optimization.
   - Frontend System Design: autocomplete, infinite scroll, real-time, large datasets.
   - Product Thinking (behavioral): collaboration with designers/PMs, balancing technical vs business needs.
   - Team lunch (evaluative).
   - Hiring Manager final.
companies.notes:
Watch out for:
- Vanilla JS / DOM heavy. Apple cares less about React syntax, more about fundamentals. Practice GreatFrontEnd's vanilla JS questions.
- Bug Hunt is unique. You navigate unfamiliar codebase under time pressure. Practice with open-source projects.
- Product Thinking is scenario-based: 'You disagreed with a designer about X — walk me through it.'
- Privacy + craft + performance are recurring themes — mention proactively.
- Team-based hiring means each team has different needs — ask your recruiter about the specific team.
- Compensation is lower than other FAANG but the culture/craft attracts people who care.

Your edge: 700ms to 150ms perf story is gold for Web Performance round. Production token/basket debug experience maps to Bug Hunt. CEO-direct collaboration shows Product Thinking maturity.

Prep specifically: drill vanilla JS polyfills to 2-min flat each. Clone a small open-source project, navigate it, find a bug. Watch CSS-Tricks for Apple-style craft conversations.

companies.name: Monzo
companies.loopStructure:
4-5 weeks typical.
1. Recruiter screen.
2. Take-home (async, your IDE, your language). Spec published publicly.
3. Walkthrough (60 min): review submission with senior engineer; defend every decision.
4. Live problem-solving (no AI in live; AI allowed on take-home with disclosure).
5. Behavioral (60 min).
companies.notes:
Watch out for:
- AI on take-home is allowed but defend every line.
- They publish their interview process publicly — read it.
- Backend-heavy company; senior FE rare and highly compensated.
- Culture round probes ethical instincts in fintech.

Your edge: Lloyds digitization story translates directly.

companies.name: Revolut
companies.loopStructure:
3-5 weeks.
1. Recruiter screen.
2. Take-home (6-8 hours; days to submit): build small service with tests + docs.
3. Take-home review (45-60 min): 'Why this architecture?' 'How would this scale 10x?' 'Where are the failure modes?'
4. Live coding (45-60 min): fintech flavor (transaction processors, currency conversion).
5. System design (mid+).
6. Bar raiser / team fit.
companies.notes:
Watch out for:
- Rushed take-home is #1 rejection reason. Don't ship until tests pass and README is good.
- Stack: Java/Kotlin BE, React/TypeScript FE on Kubernetes.
- 'Measurable outcomes' language preferred — user growth, conversion, cost per transaction.
- Fast culture — they ship a lot.

Your edge: Your numerical bullets (20% conversion, 700ms to 150ms, 50% code dedup) match their language exactly.

companies.name: Deliveroo
companies.loopStructure:
1. Recruiter screen.
2. Take-home (async, NO AI — AI-generated submissions rejected outright).
3. Live coding (60 min, paired — NO AI). Build a production-ready UI.
4. Behavioral (Deliveroo Values).
companies.notes:
Watch out for:
- AI is BANNED in live coding. AI-generated take-homes = rejection.
- Async-friendly process.
- Communication-heavy. 'Engineering is collaborative — so is the interview.'
- Their public values are evaluated.

Your edge: Collaboration stories (CEO/CTO, offshore team) play well here.

companies.name: Meta London
companies.loopStructure:
4-8 weeks.
1. Recruiter screen.
2. Technical phone screen (1-2x coding).
3. Onsite (4-5 hours):
   - Coding round 1 (traditional CoderPad).
   - AI-Assisted Coding round (E4-E5+ since Oct 2025): 60 min, multi-file codebase, AI chat panel, optional use.
   - Frontend System Design (build at scale).
   - Behavioral (Meta Values: ownership, impact, move fast).
companies.notes:
Watch out for:
- AI-Assisted round is HERE. Practice methodology — read first, run tests, narrate, verify.
- One thematic question with multiple stages — pacing matters.
- Three scenario types: build feature / extend partial / debug broken.
- Graded on judgment, not AI usage volume.

Your edge: AI-first delivery experience prepares you. Interviewer will appreciate production AI use, not just interview use.
